newsitem.title: CHINA: HK parliament in showdown with labour.
newsitem.headline: HK parliament in showdown with labour.

text.p: Hong Kong's China-appointed parliament is set to show its colours in a showdown with unions over a bill that would scuttle labour rights laws.

The Provisional Legislative Council, meeting on Wednesday, was widely expected to strike down at least four of seven laws enacted shortly before China took back the 156-year-old British colony on July 1.
Outside the legislative building, over 80 protesters from labour, Christian and Filipino groups shouted slogans and waved banners denouncing the council's debate inside.
"Hands off labour rights", "Shame on heavy-handed tactics against Hong Kong workers", "Say no to abolition of labour rights", the protesters shouted.
The issue is one of several entangling the post-colonial leader Tung Chee-hwa, his government and the unelected legislature.
The other quarrels are over his plan to harden up sedition laws, his bill to deport child illegal immigrants and an election law blueprint that would hamper pro-democracy forces.
Wednesday's debate and vote seemed certain to test the mettle of Hong Kong's embryonic free trade union movement led by pro-democracy firebrand and ex-legislator Lee Cheuk-yan.
It would also set a precedent.
If the new legislature can roll back one set of pre-handover laws passed by the disbanded, elected Legislative Council, it could attack a whole raft of old legislation, analysts said.
The government wants the labour laws suspended till the end of October to give it time to table counter-legislation, arguing that the laws will harm Hong Kong's economic competitiveness.
The key rights that will go are the right of unions to bargain collectively with employers on wages and benefits on behalf of employees, and the right to use union funds for political activity.

Lee, a former elected legislator ousted along with the rest of the pro-democracy bloc when China installed the provisional legislature on July 1, said he did not expect to win the present showdown but he vowed to keep up the fight.

"Within the establishment now -- both in the provisional legislature and the Executive Council -- are predominantly business interests," said Lee, secretary general of the Confederation of Trade Unions.

"So we are not too optimistic that it is possible to stop the suspension of the laws. But it's very important to keep the debate going and that the workers' voice can be heard in the community, so there can be a balance," he said on local radio.
Leader of the protesters Leung Yiu-chung vowed to carry on his fight. "No matter what outcome we have today, as we are the activists of the labour unions, we will never give up."
Leung's protest group then proceeded to the office of Hong Kong leader Tung Chee-hwa where they handed over a list of 13,000 signatures opposing the move.
But Tung defended his government's move at a public function and said the laws at issue were in question.
"Now what has happened is that these laws were rushed through without proper consultation, without really very seriously studying into the implications," Tung said.

"So I think it is right for these laws to be frozen and that we would study them carefully, consult the public and do what is right in the long-term interest of Hong Kong." The rights enshrined in the jeopardised laws are in line with international labour conventions. Hong Kong's constitution, the Basic Law, says the territory should apply standards set in those conventions, and some legal experts say the suspension could spark a constitutional crisis.
